title: Are We There Yet??
full_review:
A smooth-talking skirt-chaser gets more than he bargained for when he volunteers to taxi his girlfriend's two children from Portland, Ore., to Vancouver, British Columbia, in the leaden road comedy "Are We There Yet?" (Columbia).

Ice Cube stars as Nick Persons, a former minor-league ballplayer and major-league ladies' man who runs a sports memorabilia shop in the Pacific Northwest.

As an avowed bachelor, Nick possesses a deep-seated dislike of kids -- "they're like cockroaches, except you can't squish 'em" -- which supplies the story's conflict when he falls for pretty divorcee Suzanne (Nia Long) with two rug rats (Philip Daniel Bolden and Aleisha Allen) at home.

For their part, the kids are under the delusion that their deadbeat dad will come back and that they'll again be a happy family. To ensure that their mom stays off the dating market, they scare away prospective suitors; one unlucky gentleman caller gets pelted with paint balls.

When Suzanne is called out of town for business (she is a party planner and is catering a New Year's Eve shindig in Vancouver), Nick -- hoping to score some points -- offers to baby-sit and ferry the mischievous youngsters to Canada in time for a reuniting round of "Auld Lang Syne."

Of course, all this goes against Nick's better judgment, not to mention the advice of his computer-animated conscience, a Satchel Paige bobblehead doll (voiced by Tracy Morgan) he keeps on his dashboard.

After attempts by plane and train prove disastrous, Nick bites the bullet and piles the tykes into his prize possession, a shiny, souped-up SUV, which you just know will be scrap metal by the end credits.

Anything that could go wrong does, as the terror twins use everything in their repertoire to make the trip a living hell for Nick.

While Ice Cube has undeniable charisma, the film runs out of gas early, leaving viewers to endure 94 minutes of scatological sight gags and unfunny -- and often mean-spirited -- mishaps (making it unsuitable for younger adolescents). You know you're in for a bumpy ride when the film's idea of a punch line involves carsickness and kicks to the groin. The picture's sadistic slapstick echoes that of "Home Alone," but at least in that movie the bungling burglars were getting their just rewards. Here, Nick is victimized for no apparent reason other than to wring a few cheap laughs out of the movie's flat-tire script.

Director Brian Levant tries to elicit some sympathy for the kids with some late sentimentality and by making one of them asthmatic, but for much of the film they come across as selfish, ill-mannered brats.

Buried somewhere beneath the potty jokes is a sincere message about the importance of family and parenthood, but by the time it surfaces the question being asked is not "Are we there yet?" but "Is it over yet?"

The film contains recurring crude humor and comic violence, as well as some mildly crass language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
